title: 58: Coalescing & Unlink
desc: Goal: Learn how glibc merges adjacent free chunks to reduce fragmentation. When a chunk is freed, the allocator checks its neighbors: if the previous chunk is free (backward consolidation) or the next chunk is free (forward consolidation), they are merged via the unlink macro. Corrupting unlink metadata was the basis of classic heap exploits.
source: // guard prevents C from merging with top
free(B);  // B goes to unsorted bin
// A+B are now one big free chunk

logs.msg: Fragmentation is the enemy of allocators. When two adjacent chunks are both free, glibc merges them into one larger chunk -- this is called coalescing. The unlink macro removes a chunk from its bin so it can be absorbed into its neighbor. Let's watch it happen.
malloc(128) -- chunk A: 136 bytes (128 data + 8 header). Size field = 0x89 (136 | PREV_INUSE). These are too large for fast bins, so when freed they will go to the unsorted bin and can be coalesced.

malloc(128) -- chunk B: 136 bytes, right after A. B's P bit is set (A is in use). Note: fast bins are NOT coalesced, but chunks this size (> 64 bytes) go through the normal free path which does coalesce.
malloc(128) -- chunk C: 136 bytes, right after B. Three contiguous chunks are now allocated.
malloc(16) -- a guard chunk after C. Without this, freeing C would just merge it into the top chunk (the wilderness). The guard keeps C as a distinct free chunk.

free(B) -- B goes to the unsorted bin (too large for fast bins). The allocator checks B's neighbors: A is still in use (P bit of B = 1), and C is still in use (P bit of the chunk after C = 1). No coalescing occurs. B's prev_size in the next chunk's header is set to 136 so C knows B's size.

free(A) -- the allocator checks A's forward neighbor: B is FREE! Forward consolidation triggers. The unlink macro removes B from the unsorted bin (B->fd->bk = B->bk; B->bk->fd = B->fd), then A absorbs B. The merged chunk has size 136 + 136 = 272 bytes.

The unlink macro performs: FD = B->fd; BK = B->bk; FD->bk = BK; BK->fd = FD. In old glibc (pre-2.3.6), there were NO checks on FD/BK. By corrupting fd/bk in a free chunk, an attacker could write an arbitrary value to an arbitrary address -- the classic "unlink exploit" (unsafe unlink).

Coalescing reduces fragmentation by merging adjacent free chunks. The unlink macro removes a chunk from its doubly-linked bin list during consolidation. Modern glibc validates fd/bk pointers (FD->bk == P && BK->fd == P), but corrupting the size/prev_size fields to fake adjacency is still an active technique in heap exploitation.

winMsg: You watched forward consolidation merge two adjacent free chunks via the unlink macro. Understanding coalescing is key to exploits like unsafe unlink, House of Einherjar, and overlapping chunks.
